content.text:
The original double border was:

1. A 1px CSS border on `#panel`.
2. Windows’ native DWM window border, colored through `DWMWA_BORDER_COLOR`.

Commit `1113ee3` removed the CSS border by commenting it out; DWM’s border remained. That comment also accidentally disabled the panel’s radius and shadow, which commit `7e2ad15` restored while keeping the CSS border disabled.

The current black/white mode is different: DWM’s border is suppressed, and the visible hairline is a CSS inset shadow. So the corner gap you see now isn’t the original double-border issue.
will it be resolved if we had removed the 2. Windows’ native DWM window border instead for opaque windows?

For the **original double border**, yes: suppressing DWM’s border and keeping the CSS border would have left one CSS-drawn outline.

For the **current black/white corner gap**, no. Opaque mode already sets DWM’s border to `NONE` in [host.rs](C:/Users/mshab/Projects/nex/apps/core/src/overlay/host.rs:3027). The visible hairline is the CSS inset shadow, so changing the DWM setting won’t affect it. The fix needs to adjust that CSS hairline relative to the hard rounded region clip.
we could easily resolve this if we just use only the css border instead right?

Yes, CSS is the right place for the rounded outline. In black and white modes, DWM’s border is already disabled, and the visible hairline is currently a CSS inset shadow.

A plain `border: 1px` may still get clipped by the native rounded region and can affect the panel’s content sizing. A 1px CSS border drawn on an absolutely positioned overlay just inside the panel would follow the rounded corners without changing layout. It would sit about 1px inward from the outside edge.
then implement this fix

I’ll replace the black/white inset shadow with a 1px CSS outline inset by 1px and rounded to 7px. That keeps the stroke inside the native clip and avoids changing panel layout. I’ll also use the repository’s commit message skill when staging the change.

content.text:
You can have clean corners like Settings. The current overlay is built with separate layers that disagree at the edge.

Settings’ window edge is composed as part of its native Windows frame. Nex draws its 1px border in the WebView, then Windows clips the host and WebView with a separate rounded region. The CSS radius is in CSS pixels; the region radius is in physical pixels. In opaque modes, Nex also tells DWM to suppress its border. Those separate steps can leave the CSS stroke clipped or misaligned at the corners.

The relevant code is the [CSS border](C:\Users\mshab\Projects\nex\apps\core\assets\style.css:2287) and the [native region and DWM border handling](C:\Users\mshab\Projects\nex\apps\core\src\overlay\host.rs:3027). My last change moved the CSS stroke to the panel edge, but kept this layered setup, so it couldn’t guarantee Settings-like corners.

To match that edge cleanly, one layer needs to own both the rounded outline and border—ideally the native Windows frame—with the WebView content fitted inside it. CSS alone can look close, but it remains subject to the separate native clip.
what issues will we face if we do these
I’ll check the Windows frame behavior and map the likely risks to Nex’s popup and WebView setup.

The biggest risk is that **Windows won’t apply its rounded corners while Nex uses window regions**. Microsoft documents window regions as a reason a window cannot receive DWM-rounded corners. Nex sets regions on both the host and the WebView, so a native-corner path would have to remove those clips. ([Windows rounded-corner guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/desktop/modernize/ui/apply-rounded-corners), [Nex region code](C:\Users\mshab\Projects\nex\apps\core\src\overlay\host.rs:3042))

That leaves a few practical risks:

- **Square corners if Windows declines to round the popup.** DWM’s corner preference is a request, not a guarantee. It can also omit rounding in some environments, such as virtual machines or remote sessions. We’d need to keep a fallback for those cases. ([Microsoft’s corner guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/desktop/modernize/ui/apply-rounded-corners))
- **Frame behavior and sizing changes.** Nex currently strips caption-frame styles from its popup. Getting DWM to draw a border may require changing those styles; that could affect the client bounds, positioning, hit testing, shadows, or the first show’s alignment. Simply turning the DWM border back on may also bring back the unwanted frame ring.
- **Less control over the outline.** DWM offers standard corner preferences, not a CSS radius value. Its border color also needs to be updated for the app’s theme and active/inactive state. The result may look more like Windows’ standard frame than an exact 1px, 8px CSS outline. ([DWM border and corner attributes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/dwmapi/ne-dwmapi-dwmwindowattribute))
- **Windows version fallback.** These DWM attributes require Windows 11 build 22000 or later, so older Windows versions need another edge treatment. ([DWM attribute support](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/dwmapi/ne-dwmapi-dwmwindowattribute))

I’d limit any native-frame experiment to the **opaque modes** and leave the working glass path alone. The main tradeoff is a more Windows-native edge when DWM supports it, with a fallback needed where it doesn’t.
what if we do it only on the opaqu windows and leave the glass window as it is?
Yes, that can isolate the change. I’ll verify how Nex switches the same window between opaque and glass modes, since that determines what must be toggled when the user changes backgrounds.
